feature: per-port `protocol:` inspectability / TLS-pinning passthrough (M5 P1 — #233 + #238 + #239/PR #262, re-run on PR #264's tip)

journeys.rationale: The capability floor for every other journey: a user who has read the docs can write an egress policy file, hand it to a new sandbox, and read the resulting posture back. If this fails nothing below is meaningful.

journeys.rationale: The headline promise: one named port of one exact host can be declared exempt from interception for a client that pins certificates, and the exemption is per port. Everything in core/deep about the hatch presumes a user can get one declared at all.

journeys.rationale: Discoverability of the audit surface itself (predicted flag D7 in the previous campaign, fixed in place on this tip). Someone auditing a machine asks 'is anything on this sandbox bypassing the firewall?' and must land on the surface that answers it rather than concluding from an unrelated summary that nothing is wrong.

steps.expect: the sandbox is created with those firewall settings

steps.intent: you have inherited this machine and must answer, for audit-me, the question 'is any traffic escaping this sandbox without being inspected?' — find izba's answer
steps.expect: izba reports that one specific port of one specific host is exempt from inspection, rather than leaving you to conclude from a quiet overview that nothing is

journeys.rationale: The reviewed authoring route has to be reachable: the project file can describe the firewall, and izba can show that description as a pending, reviewable change. Every review-gate journey below builds on this.

Six deep journeys are worthless if this does not hold, so it gates rather than each of them re-proving it.

apiVersion: izba.dev/v1alpha1
kind: Sandbox
spec:
  image: alpine:3.20
  egress:
    enforce: true
    allow:
      - host: pinned.vendor.example
        ports:
          - 80
          - port: 443
            protocol: tcp
      - host: api.vendor.example
        ports:
          - port: 8000
            protocol: http

steps.intent: type {workspace} into the Workspace field, 'gui-pin1' into the Name field, and 'alpine:3.20' into the Image field, then click Create to create a new sandbox from this workspace
steps.expect: the create finishes without an error banner and a sandbox named gui-pin1 appears in the sandbox list

steps.intent: open the gui-pin1 sandbox's detail view, go to the view that shows which hosts it is allowed to reach, and work out whether the firewall is on and whether any single port there is exempt from inspection
steps.expect: the view states the firewall's on/off posture and one host row carries a visible message about one of its individual ports, naming what that port gives up

journeys.rationale: The structural promise of #238: opening one more port on a host that already has an exempt port must NOT extend the exemption to it. This is the whole point of declaring inspectability per port rather than per host.

source.ref: `izba policy allow` help: 'A granted port is always inspected: it never inherits a `protocol: tcp` pinning passthrough declared for some other port of the same host'

steps.intent: create a sandbox called inherit-no for this directory on the alpine:3.20 image whose firewall allows the host pinned.vendor.example on port 443 only, with that port exempted from interception for a certificate-pinning client
steps.expect: the sandbox is created with that single exempt port

steps.intent: the same vendor also serves a metrics endpoint on port 9000 — grant inherit-no access to port 9000 of pinned.vendor.example from the command line
steps.expect: the grant succeeds and izba echoes the access level it granted

steps.intent: check whether that newly granted port is exempt from inspection too, or whether only the original one is
steps.expect: only the originally exempted port is treated as exempt; the newly granted port is inspected like any other

journeys.rationale: A grant aimed at one port narrows the whole host entry's access, which silently switches off an exemption declared on a different port. The grant echo must say so at the moment it happens rather than leaving it to a command nobody has a reason to run.

source.ref: PR #264 commit 'fix(cli): stop stating an egress posture the firewall is not enforcing' — CORE-2: 'The echo now names the dormant port and how to restore it'

steps.intent: create a sandbox called dormant-echo for this directory on the alpine:3.20 image whose firewall allows the host pinned.vendor.example on port 443, exempted from interception for a certificate-pinning client
steps.expect: the sandbox is created with that exempt port

steps.intent: that vendor also has a docs site on port 9000 which this sandbox should only be able to READ from — grant dormant-echo read-only access to port 9000 of pinned.vendor.example
steps.expect: izba grants it and, in the same breath, tells you that this narrowing has taken the exempt port out of effect and how to get it back

journeys.rationale: An exemption on a host that is only allowed to read is declared but dormant — an opaque connection carries no HTTP method, so a read-only grant never authorizes one. The audit surface must report it as not in effect rather than as a live hole, and must say what would make it live.

source.ref: CLAUDE.md 'Inspectability is DECLARED per PORT': 'both render a pinned port on a NARROWER-than-read-write row as NOT in effect rather than live'

steps.intent: create a sandbox called dormant-show for this directory on the alpine:3.20 image whose firewall allows the host pinned.vendor.example on port 443 — exempted from interception — but restricts that host to read-only access
steps.expect: the create command finishes without an error

steps.intent: ask izba what dormant-show's firewall allows, and work out from its answer whether that exempt port is actually in effect right now
steps.expect: izba states that the exemption is not in effect on that port and names the change that would put it in effect

journeys.rationale: A log-only sandbox restricts nothing, so a declared exemption there is inert — nothing is being terminated, so nothing is being spliced. Reporting the allow-list bare with a live exemption warning would read as a default-deny firewall with exactly one hole: the safe-looking misstatement, on the one surface that reveals posture.

source.ref: PR #264 commit 'fix(cli): stop stating an egress posture the firewall is not enforcing' — CORE-1

steps.intent: create a sandbox called logonly for this directory on the alpine:3.20 image with firewall settings that are LOG-ONLY — everything is still allowed out and merely recorded — but which nonetheless list the host pinned.vendor.example on port 443 with that port declared exempt from interception
steps.expect: the sandbox is created and izba accepts the log-only settings

steps.intent: ask izba what logonly's firewall is actually doing, and decide from its answer whether that sandbox is restricted with one exception, or not restricted at all
steps.expect: izba says plainly that all egress is allowed and that the listed hosts are not in force, and describes the declared exemption as inert rather than as a live bypass

journeys.rationale: The exemption is matched against the name the client actually asks for, so it is only meaningful on an exactly-named host. A wildcard must be refused with an actionable message rather than quietly honoured or quietly ignored.

source.ref: CLAUDE.md: 'The TLS-pinning hatch is an EXPLICIT `protocol: tcp` on an EXACT host (a wildcard is a parse error)'

steps.intent: you want every subdomain of vendor.example to reach its own TLS untouched on port 443, so write firewall settings that name the hosts as a one-label wildcard under vendor.example with port 443 exempted from interception, and try to create a sandbox called wild-pin for this directory on the alpine:3.20 image with them
steps.expect: izba refuses the settings and its message explains that the exemption has to name each host exactly, rather than silently accepting or silently ignoring the wildcard

journeys.rationale: The restriction is asymmetric on purpose: asking for MORE inspection only ever narrows what is permitted, so a wildcard host may ask that an unusual port be policed at the HTTP layer even though it may not ask for an exemption. A user who met the wildcard refusal must not conclude that no per-port setting works on a wildcard.

source.ref: CLAUDE.md: 'The axis may only widen' + `--policy` help ('`protocol: http` polices a non-web port at L7')

steps.intent: create a sandbox called wild-http for this directory on the alpine:3.20 image whose firewall lets it reach any single-label subdomain of svc.example on port 8443, and asks izba to police that port at the HTTP layer as well
steps.expect: izba accepts these settings — unlike the exemption, asking for more inspection on a wildcard is allowed

steps.intent: read back what wild-http's firewall allows and confirm izba records that extra policing against the port you asked for
steps.expect: the report names port 8443 as inspected

journeys.rationale: A typo'd value for a per-port setting must be refused naming the values that exist — silently dropping it would leave a port the user believes is exempt (or believes is policed) behaving the other way.

source.ref: docs/superpowers/plans/2026-08-18-m5-p1-inspectability.md — parse_protocol's error names the valid set; README 'Unknown keys anywhere in policy.yaml are rejected with an error naming the key and its valid alternatives'

steps.intent: write firewall settings for a sandbox called bad-value on the alpine:3.20 image that allow the host pinned.vendor.example on port 443 and try to describe that port's handling with the word 'ssl', then try to create the sandbox with them
steps.expect: izba refuses and its message tells you which words that setting actually accepts

journeys.rationale: A misspelled key inside a port entry must be refused naming the keys that belong there. A silently ignored key is a security footgun in the quiet direction: the user believes they declared something and nothing was declared.

source.ref: README: 'Unknown keys anywhere in `policy.yaml` are rejected with an error naming the key and its valid alternatives — a typo can never silently widen egress scope'

steps.intent: write firewall settings for a sandbox called bad-key on the alpine:3.20 image that allow the host pinned.vendor.example on port 443 and, when spelling out how that port should be handled, misspell the setting's name as 'protokol'; try to create the sandbox with them
steps.expect: izba refuses and names the keys that are actually allowed inside a port entry, instead of accepting the file with the setting quietly dropped

journeys.rationale: One port must have one answer. Listing the same port twice with contradicting handling has to be refused naming both, because resolving it silently either way is how a port reported as inspected ends up spliced.

source.ref: PR #264 commit 'fix(core): refuse a port declared twice with conflicting protocols' (Greptile P1 on PR #260)

steps.intent: write firewall settings for a sandbox called dup-port on the alpine:3.20 image that allow the host pinned.vendor.example and, in that host's port list, mention port 443 twice — once plainly and once declared exempt from interception — then try to create the sandbox with them
steps.expect: izba refuses the contradiction and its message names the port and both of the things that were said about it, rather than quietly picking one

journeys.rationale: The other half of the per-port setting: an internal service on a non-web port can be asked for MORE policing than it gets by default, and the audit surface must confirm that against the port it applies to.

source.ref: README policy.yaml example: `- port: 8000 / protocol: http  # police this port at L7 too (80/443 already are)`

steps.intent: create a sandbox called probe-8000 for this directory on the alpine:3.20 image whose firewall lets it reach internal.svc.example on port 8000, and which asks izba to apply its HTTP-level rules to that port too rather than treating it as opaque traffic
steps.expect: the sandbox is created with those settings

steps.intent: read back what probe-8000's firewall allows and confirm izba recorded that request against port 8000
steps.expect: the report marks port 8000 as inspected

journeys.rationale: Back-compatibility promise: the older spelling, where the handling is stated once for a whole host entry instead of per port, still parses and still means what it always meant. An upgrading operator must not have their shipped file change posture underneath them.

source.ref: `izba create --policy` help: 'The legacy entry-level `protocol:` spelling still parses and applies to EVERY port of that entry'

steps.intent: you are carrying forward a firewall file written before izba let you say things about individual ports: it allows the host pinned.vendor.example on port 443 and states — once, for the whole host entry rather than for the port — that its traffic is to be passed through untouched for a certificate-pinning client. Write that older-style file and create a sandbox called legacy-pin for this directory on the alpine:3.20 image with it
steps.expect: izba accepts the older-style file and the sandbox ends up with port 443 of that host exempt from interception, exactly as the file always meant

steps.intent: read back what legacy-pin's firewall allows and confirm the exemption is reported against port 443
steps.expect: the report names the exempt port and what it gives up

journeys.rationale: Editing the allow-list elsewhere must neither drop nor relocate an existing exemption. The set of exempt ports must be exactly the set someone deliberately wrote one for.

source.ref: CLAUDE.md: 'EgressPolicyConfig::allow (and every other mutator, for every caller) appends a port that structurally cannot inherit a sibling port's hatch'

steps.intent: create a sandbox called survive-edit for this directory on the alpine:3.20 image whose firewall allows the host pinned.vendor.example on port 443 with that port exempt from interception for a certificate-pinning client
steps.expect: the sandbox is created with that exempt port

steps.intent: your build now also needs to fetch from a completely different host — grant survive-edit access to registry.other.example
steps.expect: the grant succeeds and izba echoes the access level

steps.intent: check that the unrelated grant did not disturb the vendor host's exemption
steps.expect: the vendor host still has its exemption on port 443 and the new host has none

journeys.rationale: The asymmetry check: if an exemption can be declared, a user must be able to retire it and see the audit surface stop reporting a bypass. Nothing in the CLI authors an exemption, so removal is the only exemption-related edit it can make.

source.ref: `izba policy block` help ('HOST:PORT removes exactly that port; auto-reloads'); `izba policy show` help (the audit surface)

steps.intent: create a sandbox called retire-pin for this directory on the alpine:3.20 image whose firewall allows the host pinned.vendor.example on port 443 alone, with that port exempt from interception
steps.expect: the sandbox is created with that exempt port

steps.intent: the pinning client has been retired — take away retire-pin's access to that vendor host entirely from the command line
steps.expect: izba removes it

steps.intent: confirm that nothing on retire-pin is exempt from inspection any more
steps.expect: the vendor host is gone from what the sandbox may reach, and the audit surface no longer reports any bypass

journeys.rationale: Quietness is a promise too: a firewall that declares nothing unusual must read as ordinary, so that the one time a warning does appear it means something. A surface that decorates every policy trains operators to ignore it.

source.ref: docs/superpowers/plans/2026-08-18-m5-p1-inspectability.md — the renderer is silent when a port declares nothing

steps.intent: create a sandbox called plain-fw for this directory on the alpine:3.20 image whose firewall is on and allows just the two hosts api.vendor.example and registry.other.example
steps.expect: the create command finishes without an error

steps.intent: read back what plain-fw's firewall allows and judge whether izba is flagging anything unusual about it
steps.expect: the two hosts and their web ports are listed plainly, with no warning markers about inspection or bypass

journeys.rationale: A command-line grant applies immediately with no review, while the same change made through the project file goes through a gate. A user must be able to find out that the two routes differ — otherwise they will believe the gate protects every path.

source.ref: README izba.yml section: 'That is the only authoring route with the `⚠ weakens egress` gate in front of it; `izba policy allow` and a hand-edited `policy.yaml` both apply immediately, unreviewed.'

steps.intent: write this project's izba.yml so that it describes a sandbox called ungated on the alpine:3.20 image with its firewall switched on and allowing only the host api.vendor.example, then create that sandbox from this project directory so the two agree
steps.expect: the create command finishes without an error

steps.intent: someone now needs one more host — grant ungated access to registry.other.example straight from the command line, without touching the project file
steps.expect: izba applies the grant immediately, without asking anyone to review it

steps.intent: check what izba now thinks about the relationship between this project's file and the sandbox's actual settings
steps.expect: izba reports that the sandbox's live settings have moved ahead of the project file — the grant went in without passing through the review step the project-file route uses

journeys.rationale: Declaring an exemption is documented as something you do by editing the sandbox's own policy file and reloading — there is no CLI flag for it. The reload must confirm WHICH file it re-read, so an operator who edited a stray copy is not told 'success' about a file izba never looked at.

source.ref: PR #264 commit 'fix(cli): name the reloaded policy path and warn --follow never exits' (DEEP-2); `izba policy reload` help names the managed file's location

steps.intent: create a sandbox called reload-pin for this directory on the alpine:3.20 image whose firewall allows the host pinned.vendor.example on port 443, with nothing exempted yet
steps.expect: the sandbox is created with the firewall on

steps.intent: a certificate-pinning client now has to run in reload-pin — change that sandbox's firewall so port 443 of pinned.vendor.example reaches the vendor's own TLS untouched, and make izba pick the change up
steps.expect: izba re-reads the sandbox's settings and tells you exactly which file it read them from

journeys.rationale: Per-port attribution on the desktop surface: the warning must belong to the port that carries the exemption. A host-level annotation would misreport which port gave a control up, and a port that merely asked for extra policing must not look exempt.

source.ref: issue #239 AC 1-3 (the marker names the port; absent for http/undeclared ports)

steps.intent: create a sandbox called two-hosts for this directory on the alpine:3.20 image whose firewall is on and allows two hosts on ports 80 and 443 — example.com, whose port 443 is exempt from interception for a certificate-pinning client, and example.net, which gets no such exemption

steps.intent: ask izba's connection log what it did with that attempt
steps.expect: the attempt was refused rather than passed through — the exemption did not follow the bare address

journeys.rationale: Egress settings are a live-class change: adding an exemption to a running sandbox and reloading must take effect on the next connection without stopping anything. A user who has to restart loses their session for a firewall tweak.

source.ref: `izba policy reload` help: 'Re-read a sandbox's policy.yaml and apply it to new connections (no restart)'

steps.intent: create and start a sandbox called live-pin for this directory on the alpine:3.20 image whose firewall is on and allows the host example.com on ports 80 and 443, with nothing exempted, and confirm from inside it that https://example.com/ can be fetched
steps.expect: the sandbox is running and the fetch works

steps.intent: without stopping the sandbox, change live-pin's firewall so port 443 of example.com now reaches the site's own TLS untouched, and make izba apply it
steps.expect: izba applies the change to the running sandbox and says it takes effect on new connections

steps.intent: fetch https://example.com/ from inside the still-running sandbox again, then ask izba's connection log what it did with THAT connection
steps.expect: the newer connection was passed through rather than inspected, without the sandbox ever having been restarted

journeys.rationale: Lifecycle promise: the exemption lives in the sandbox's managed settings, not in the running process, so stopping and starting must not quietly drop it (or quietly keep enforcing an older version of it).

source.ref: CLAUDE.md disk-state invariant: managed policy.yaml is the host-only authority re-read on every start

steps.intent: create and start a sandbox called restart-pin for this directory on the alpine:3.20 image whose firewall is on, allows the host example.com on ports 80 and 443, and exempts port 443 of that host from interception
steps.expect: the sandbox is created and running with that exempt port

steps.intent: stop restart-pin and start it again
steps.expect: the sandbox comes back up

steps.intent: check that the exemption is still in place on the restarted sandbox and that the firewall is still on
steps.expect: the firewall is still enforcing and port 443 of that host is still reported as exempt

journeys.rationale: Seeding the allow-list from what a sandbox actually reached goes through the same mutator as a manual grant, so it too must append plain ports and must not disturb an existing exemption. This mutator is the one a user is least likely to inspect afterwards.

source.ref: CLAUDE.md: 'EgressPolicyConfig::allow (and every other mutator, for every caller — CLI, GUI, observed-traffic seeding) appends a port that structurally cannot inherit a sibling port's hatch'

steps.intent: create and start a sandbox called seeded for this directory on the alpine:3.20 image whose firewall is on, allows the host example.com on ports 80 and 443 with port 443 exempt from interception, and also allows example.net; from inside it fetch both https://example.com/ and https://example.net/
steps.expect: the sandbox is running and both fetches complete

steps.intent: now have izba build seeded's allow-list up from the traffic it has actually been permitting, so the list reflects real usage
steps.expect: izba reports how many observed endpoints it added and reloads the sandbox's settings

steps.intent: read back seeded's firewall and check what happened to the exempt port and to anything newly added
steps.expect: the exemption is still attached to the port it was declared on, and nothing that was added from observed traffic is exempt

journeys.rationale: Declaring a new exemption weakens the firewall even though it adds no host, opens no port and changes no access level. The review step must flag it, or the one authoring route that HAS a gate does not actually catch the change the gate exists for.

source.ref: CLAUDE.md: 'manifest::diff flags two ⚠ weakens egress transitions: a newly-declared passthrough, and losing inspection on a still-reachable port'

steps.intent: write this project's izba.yml so that it describes a sandbox called flag-new on the alpine:3.20 image whose firewall is switched on and allows the host pinned.vendor.example on port 443 with full read-write access and nothing declared about that port, then create the sandbox from this project directory so the two agree
steps.expect: the sandbox is created and its firewall matches the project file, with nothing exempt

steps.intent: a certificate-pinning client is moving into this sandbox — edit ONLY the project file so that the very same port 443 of that very same host is now exempt from interception, changing nothing else about the file, and then ask izba to show you the pending change before you apply it
steps.expect: izba shows the firewall change as pending and marks it as one that weakens the sandbox's egress protection, even though no host was added and no access level was widened

journeys.rationale: The subtler weakening: removing the one host that asked for a shared non-web port to be policed at the HTTP layer silently un-polices that port for every other host still allowed on it. The review step must flag a change that, read naively, only ever removes access.

source.ref: CLAUDE.md: 'losing inspection on a still-reachable port' is the second flagged transition

steps.intent: write this project's izba.yml so that it describes a sandbox called flag-lost on the alpine:3.20 image whose firewall is switched on and allows two internal services on the same port 8443 — svc-a.internal.example, for which you have asked izba to apply its HTTP-level rules to that port, and svc-b.internal.example, for which you have asked for nothing special — then create the sandbox from this project directory so the two agree
steps.expect: the sandbox is created and its firewall matches the project file

steps.intent: the first service has been decommissioned — edit ONLY the project file to drop svc-a.internal.example entirely, leaving the second service exactly as it was, then ask izba to show you the pending change before applying it
steps.expect: izba flags the change as weakening the sandbox's egress protection, even though it only removes a host

journeys.rationale: The warning must mean something: retiring an exemption tightens the firewall and must NOT be flagged as weakening it. A review step that flags every egress change is a review step operators learn to click through.

source.ref: docs/superpowers/plans/2026-08-18-m5-p1-inspectability.md — egress_weakens flags only the two named transitions

steps.intent: write this project's izba.yml so that it describes a sandbox called flag-quiet on the alpine:3.20 image whose firewall is switched on and allows the host pinned.vendor.example on port 443 with that port exempt from interception, then create the sandbox from this project directory so the two agree
steps.expect: the sandbox is created with that exempt port and matches the project file

steps.intent: the pinning client has been retired — edit ONLY the project file so that port 443 of that host is no longer exempt, leaving everything else exactly as it was, then ask izba to show you the pending change before applying it
steps.expect: izba lists the firewall change as pending but does NOT mark it as weakening egress protection

journeys.rationale: The only reviewed route to an exemption must actually work end to end: describe it in the project file, review it, approve it, and find it in the sandbox's managed settings — with the approval step loud about what is being given up.

source.ref: README izba.yml section (the reviewed route) + review gate: 'You cannot miss a loosened firewall'

steps.intent: write this project's izba.yml so that it describes a sandbox called gated-pin on the alpine:3.20 image whose firewall is switched on and allows the host pinned.vendor.example on port 443, with nothing declared about that port, then create the sandbox from this project directory so the two agree
steps.expect: the sandbox is created and matches the project file

steps.intent: edit the project file so that port 443 of that host is exempt from interception, then review the pending change
steps.expect: izba shows the pending firewall change and flags it as weakening egress protection

steps.intent: approve the reviewed change so it becomes the sandbox's real settings
steps.expect: izba applies it and warns, at the moment of approval, that this weakens the sandbox's egress protection

journeys.rationale: The gate is only a gate if it refuses. Approving a firewall-weakening change that nobody has looked at must fail with a message naming the missing step, not apply silently.

source.ref: README 'Review gate': `izba promote` requires the review token written by `izba diff`

steps.intent: write this project's izba.yml so that it describes a sandbox called ungated-pin on the alpine:3.20 image whose firewall is switched on and allows the host pinned.vendor.example on port 443, with nothing declared about that port, then create the sandbox from this project directory so the two agree
steps.expect: the create command finishes without an error

steps.intent: edit the project file so that port 443 of that host is exempt from interception, and then — without looking at the change first — go straight to applying it
steps.expect: izba refuses to apply the change and its message names the step that was skipped

journeys.rationale: The desktop editor's save path has no weakening review in front of it, so renaming a host that carries an exemption would move that exemption onto a host nobody declared one for. The refusal must survive a real save and a re-read, not merely look refused on screen — so this journey makes a legitimate edit alongside the refused one, and grades the saved settings.

source.ref: PR #262 'The decision (AC 4)': relocation and activation are both refused in the reducer
